subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

criteria.rationale: Talk.tsx renders the kit's Presentation with the STEPS array, a title and initialMode. It doesn't build its own navigation or stage. The shared WorkshopScene imports SceneLayer, Appear, Box, Frame and SceneProps from the kit barrel and renders every entity through Box or Frame with an id. Steps are typed as kit Step<number> and supply Scene, payload and groupKey, which Stage consumes. The demo has no private stage, nav or morph machinery.

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: All nine steps come from one map over outline.json in steps/index.ts. Each step gets the same Scene (WorkshopScene) and the same groupKey 'workshop'. Stage keys its motion.div scene wrapper on step.groupKey ?? step.id. Adjacent steps therefore keep the same mounted scene and the Scene receives a new payload. A single shared groupKey is the correct grouping for one continuously evolving scene. Entity identity is separate. The presentation-owned entityId(key) returns 'how-to-make-a-presentation:<key>'. Scene.tsx passes it as id to Box or Frame. Box and entityNode (used by Frame) forward id to motion.div layoutId, with layout set. Stage wraps the scene in a LayoutGroup. visibleEntities(beat) returns every entity whose 'at' is at or below the beat, so an entity present in consecutive steps keeps the same layoutId. All nine steps share this one path. Every ENTITY key is consumed this way, including the connection entities 'conversation' and 'pipeline' and the 'link' entities, which render as Boxes.
evidence: steps/index.ts: outline.map(... Scene: WorkshopScene, groupKey: 'workshop', payload: i + 1) covers all 9 outline entries (beat-1 to beat-9).
Stage.tsx: <motion.div key={step.groupKey ?? step.id}> inside <LayoutGroup id={namespace}> and <AnimatePresence>; <Scene payload={step.payload} />.
entities.ts: entityId = key => `how-to-make-a-presentation:${key}`; visibleEntities filters by entities[key].at <= beat.
Scene.tsx: visibleEntities(beat).map(key => ... id={entityId(key)}) on Frame or Box, keyed by key.
Box.tsx: <motion.div layout layoutId={id} ... data-entity-id={id}>; entityNode.tsx (used by Frame.tsx): same layout and layoutId={id}.

subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: Responsibilities are separated. The registry (presentations/index.ts) maps the slug to a lazy Talk import. Talk.tsx only composes Presentation, STEPS and the local CSS. Step metadata lives in outline.json, entity geometry and identity in entities.ts, rendering in steps/Scene.tsx, and styling in presentation.css. The kit holds the generic mechanisms. The public title contract is consumed: Talk passes title, and Presentation uses it as the main element's aria-label. The kit's public props and shared constants are used. Stage uses DESIGN_W, DESIGN_H, LAYOUT_T and STAGE_LAYOUT. Box and entityNode use LAYOUT_T. Appear uses ENTER_T, which uses ENTER_DELAY. I found no dead or misleading contract in the inspected source.

subcomponents.title: Entity transitions and persistent grouped scenes

criteria.rationale: Every entity primitive renders motion elements with layout and a layoutId equal to the stable entity id, plus a layout transition (LAYOUT_T). Box and Label do this directly, and entityNode (used by Arrow, Frame, Emphasis and SymbolChip) does the same. Position, size, label and emphasis changes therefore animate in place. Test I-4 checks the same DOM node persists while its state changes.

entityNode.tsx: same layout/layoutId props.
Label.tsx: motion.span with layout and layoutId.
tests/runtime.test.tsx I-4.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: Stage wraps the scene in AnimatePresence with mode='sync' inside a LayoutGroup. Each scene is an absolutely positioned inset-0 motion.div, so the outgoing scene is out of layout flow while the incoming one mounts, and both stay mounted together. The entity primitives (Box, entityNode, Label) have no initial opacity and no entrance delay, so a persisting layoutId entity is not hidden. It shares its layoutId across the two scenes and animates with LAYOUT_T. Appear is an opt-in wrapper that adds the delayed opacity, and it is not applied to the layout animation.
evidence: Stage.tsx: <LayoutGroup id={namespace}><AnimatePresence initial={false} mode="sync"><motion.div key={step.groupKey ?? step.id} style={{position:'absolute', inset:0}} …
Box.tsx and entityNode.tsx: only layout/layoutId/transition.layout, with no initial opacity or delay.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T.duration = 0.48, so ENTER_T.delay equals the layout transition duration. Appear applies ENTER_T (opacity 0 to 1, y 8 to 0) only to its wrapper's entry. The Box layout transition is LAYOUT_T with no delay, so continuing entities move immediately. The sample renders every identity-bearing entity (Box or Frame with entityId) inside Appear, so each newcomer is invisible until the delay passes. The 'edited' em has no identity and sits inside the Box.
evidence: constants.ts: LAYOUT_T.duration 0.48; ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T.duration; ENTER_T = {duration:0.24, delay: ENTER_DELAY}.
Appear.tsx: initial opacity 0, transition={ENTER_T} on the wrapper only.
Box.tsx: transition={{ layout: LAYOUT_T }} with no delay.
Scene.tsx: every visible entity is <Appear key={key}> around Box/Frame.
tests/runtime.test.tsx I-5 asserts ENTER_DELAY >= LAYOUT_T.duration and the Appear props.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: Appear defines an exit animation (opacity 0 with no delay and 0.18s duration). subcomponents.title: Fixed-canvas uniform viewport fitting

criteria.rationale: fitScale returns a single factor, min((width - 2*inset)/designW, (height - top - bottom)/designH, 1), and Stage applies it as transform: scale(scale) to a fixed-size canvas, so there is one factor on both axes with no internal reflow. The stage region is positioned with the same STAGE_LAYOUT geometry (inset: top inset bottom), so the fit is computed from the area the stage occupies. At 1280x720 browse the stage is 1232x400, giving min(1.4, 1.05, 1) = 1. At 390x844 browse the width is 342, giving 342/880 ≈ 0.39, which fits. The resize listener updates the scale (test I-19).
evidence: useFitScale.ts: fitScale and useFitScale (resize listener).
Stage.tsx: scale = useFitScale(mode, width, height); style transform scale(${scale}); stage inset built from STAGE_LAYOUT[mode].
constants.ts: STAGE_LAYOUT browse {top:100,bottom:220,inset:24}, present {top:40,bottom:120,inset:24}.
tests/runtime.test.tsx I-19: expected fit values and canvas transform scale(0.5).
judging basis: consensus-pass

votes.rationale: Talk.tsx renders the kit's Presentation with the STEPS array, a title and initialMode. It doesn't build its own navigation or stage. The shared WorkshopScene imports SceneLayer, Appear, Box, Frame and SceneProps from the kit barrel and renders every entity through Box or Frame with an id. Steps are typed as kit Step<number> and supply Scene, payload and groupKey, which Stage consumes. The demo has no private stage, nav or morph machinery.
evidence: Talk.tsx: <Presentation steps={STEPS} title="How to Use This Skill to Make a Presentation" initialMode="browse" /> imported from '../../presentation-kit'.

votes.rationale: Stage wraps the scene in AnimatePresence with mode='sync' inside a LayoutGroup. Each scene is an absolutely positioned inset-0 motion.div, so the outgoing scene is out of layout flow while the incoming one mounts, and both stay mounted together. The entity primitives (Box, entityNode, Label) have no initial opacity and no entrance delay, so a persisting layoutId entity is not hidden. It shares its layoutId across the two scenes and animates with LAYOUT_T. Appear is an opt-in wrapper that adds the delayed opacity, and it is not applied to the layout animation.

votes.rationale: The verifier reserves an ephemeral port with freePort, closes the probe, then starts vite preview with --strictPort. Readiness, however, comes from HTTP polling of that address with fetch(url), not from the child's own announcement. The only ownership check is `preview.exitCode !== null`, sampled at the top of each polling iteration before the fetch. Neither accepted mechanism is present: there is no readiness read from the child's output, and polling is not raced against the child's exit event. A server that grabbed the port between probe.close and the preview bind could answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. That is the sampled-liveness-plus-strict-port pattern the guidance rejects.

verification-tooling.rationale: freePort closes its probe before the preview is spawned with --strictPort. Readiness comes from HTTP fetch(url) polling. The only ownership check is `preview.exitCode !== null`, sampled at the top of each loop iteration before the fetch. There is no parse of the child's announced address and no race against the exit event. A stale or foreign server on the port could answer before the child's exit is observed. votes.rationale: The verifier reserves an ephemeral port with freePort, closes the probe, then starts vite preview with --strictPort. Readiness, however, comes from HTTP polling of that address with fetch(url), not from the child's own announcement. The only ownership check is `preview.exitCode !== null`, sampled at the top of each polling iteration before the fetch. Neither accepted mechanism is present: there is no readiness read from the child's output, and polling is not raced against the child's exit event. A server that grabbed the port between probe.close and the preview bind could answer the fetch before the child's exit is observed. That is the sampled-liveness-plus-strict-port pattern the guidance rejects.

results.rationale: The full file tests/integration.test.mjs (lines 1-191) shows that no test starts a preview server or browser on its own. Every preview and browser is started through the verify or inspect scripts, which call withPreview in scripts/browser-runtime.mjs. withPreview allocates its port dynamically. freePort() listens on port 0 (lines 15-21) and the port is passed to Vite with --strictPort (line 25). No test or script hardcodes a shared port. The preview is spawned as the Vite node process itself (process.execPath with node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js), not through an npm or npx wrapper. A nested finally block, which every exit path passes through, closes the browser and the browser server, then sends SIGTERM to the preview, escalates to SIGKILL after 2 s, and awaits its exit (lines 47-67). The command() watchdog (line 18) fires only when a run exceeds its limit, a scenario that neither the criterion's guidance names nor the recorded evidence shows. A tester-authored two-scene route in the disposable app then changed to a different Scene; after transition its old `third:topic` entity had exited and only `third:closing` remained. Sampling the reference step-2 newcomer showed opacity 0 through about 480 ms, then a fade beginning by 511 ms and reaching 1 by 751 ms, matching the 480 ms layout duration. The custom route uses the neutral starter CSS and was used only for departure behavior, not as evidence of generated visual polish. Evidence: AXI text in this log and `generated-step-01.png` / `generated-step-02-after-departure.png`.

**Ruling:** The sample-specific normative statement controls the sample, and the generic kit capability stays as designed. They do not contradict. The kit requirements say what persisting entities do when their state changes, and the sample is a case where continuing entities' coordinates do not change. Concretely:
1. The sample is one grouped scene with one scene component and one `group` shared by all nine steps, so the scene instance persists. Each entity has a stable ID in a single layoutId namespace.
2. Each step's payload is the previous step's entity set plus new entities. Every continuing entity keeps identical coordinates and size in all later payloads.

3. Continuing entities may change non-geometric state only where the spec calls for it: the partial/full control value, the verify node's check status resolving to pass (step 7), the "edited" flag on a card (step 8), and the reveal frame (new entity, step 9).
4. Containers such as the tray get their final geometry when they first appear (step 3), so later cards land inside it without resizing or moving it. The tray stays unframed in step 6.

5. The generic kit still supports and unit/component-tests position, size, label and emphasis morphs, using test fixtures with moving entities. I-4 is met by the kit tests plus the sample's identity definitions. The sample is not required to demonstrate positional morphs.
6. A component test over all nine sample payloads asserts that the entity set accumulates (superset at each step) and that continuing IDs have invariant coordinates. A negative case is included.

- **Not exercised:** live prompt/question sequencing, user-selected partial-detail continuation, optional ASCII mockup confirmation, confirmation-before-write behavior, already-scaffolded anchor detection by the skill, actual skill-authored new presentation generation, ambiguous modification target listing/choice, and the skill agent’s own failure-repair conversation. Reason: `SKILL.md` is a procedural LLM instruction and this session provides no separate invocation/transcript harness; no human input is available. Direct scaffold/runtime behaviors were still exercised; these specific dialogue behaviors remain unverified.
- **Not exercised:** physical touchscreen hardware. The test plan allows equivalent browser input synthesis; AXI dispatched a horizontal touch gesture and one-step navigation was observed.

- **Not exercised:** publishing/export/hosting, paid services, credentials, exhaustive malformed-project combinations, very short viewports that could collapse fit scale to zero, or a full generic route matrix. Publishing/export/hosting are explicitly out of scope; the rest were excluded as nonessential or beyond targeted risk after the named paths were checked.
